```{r}
#| label: setup
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

table_dir <- file.path("..", "outputs", "tables")
figure_dir <- file.path("..", "outputs", "figures")
```

## Data Preparation Details

The analysis uses `data/raw/BirthsAndFertilityRatesAnnual.csv`, obtained from
the Singapore Department of Statistics (SingStat) births and fertility register.
The raw file is in wide format: each row is a named demographic series and each
column is a calendar year. The preparation script `scripts/01_prepare_data.R`
performs the following steps:

1. Reads the raw CSV and identifies year columns by pattern matching.
2. Pivots to long format with columns `Measure`, `Year`, and `Observed`.
3. Parses year columns as integers and observed values as numeric.
4. Filters to the two analysis series (Total Fertility Rate and Total Live
   Births) by exact name match after trimming whitespace.
5. Constructs a `tsibble` time series object indexed by `Measure` and `Year`.

The validation script `scripts/01_validate_data.R` then confirms the
cleaned data meet all required quality checks before any analysis proceeds.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-clean-head
#| tbl-cap: "First ten rows of the cleaned analysis-ready series"
clean_series <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "clean_birth_fertility_series.csv"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE)
kable(head(clean_series, 10), digits = 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-clean-tail
#| tbl-cap: "Last ten rows of the cleaned analysis-ready series"
kable(tail(clean_series, 10), digits = 4)
```

```{r}

#| tbl-cap: "Series summary"
series_summary <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "series_summary.csv"),
                           show_col_types = FALSE)
kable(series_summary, digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-validation
#| tbl-cap: "Automated data validation checks"
validation_checks <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "data_validation_checks.csv"),
                              show_col_types = FALSE)
kable(validation_checks)
```

All six validation checks passed with no corrections required. The analysis
window is 1960–2025, yielding 66 annual observations per series. No imputation
or interpolation was performed.

## Additional Exploratory Plots

### Level ACF

```{r}
#| label: fig-level-acf
#| fig-cap: "Sample ACF of both series at the original (level) scale."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure_dir, "level_acf.png"))
```

The level ACFs (@fig-level-acf) decay very slowly and monotonically, with
virtually every lag exceeding the 95% confidence bands. This pattern is
characteristic of an integrated (I(1)) or near-unit-root process. Modelling
at the level without differencing would leave strong autocorrelation in the
residuals, violating the white-noise assumption of ARIMA models.

### First-Difference ACF

```{r}
#| label: fig-diff-acf
#| fig-cap: "Sample ACF after one order of first differencing."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure_dir, "first_difference_acf.png"))
```

After first differencing (@fig-diff-acf):

- **TFR:** A positive spike at lag 1 (ACF1 ≈ 0.37) remains within the
  confidence band boundary. This single significant lag motivates the MA(1)
  term in the ARIMA(0,1,1) selection.
- **Total Live Births:** No spikes beyond lag 0 are significant, consistent
  with the ARIMA(0,1,0) (random walk) selection. The differenced series
  behaves as approximately white noise.

## Model Equations

### Benchmark Models

**Naïve model:**
$$
\hat{y}_{T+h|T} = y_T \quad \text{for all } h \geq 1
$$
The point forecast is always the last observed value. Prediction intervals
widen at rate $\sqrt{h}$.

**Drift model (random walk with drift):**
$$
y_t = y_{t-1} + \hat{b} + \varepsilon_t, \quad \varepsilon_t \sim \text{WN}(0, \sigma^2)
$$
where $\hat{b}$ is estimated as the average of all historical first differences:
$$
\hat{b} = \frac{y_T - y_1}{T - 1}
$$
For TFR: $\hat{b} = -0.082$ (SE = 0.021).
For Total Live Births: $\hat{b} = -356$ births per year (SE = 371).

### Deterministic Trend Model

$$
y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot t + \varepsilon_t, \quad \varepsilon_t \sim \text{WN}(0, \sigma^2)
$$

For TFR: $\hat{\beta}_0 = 4.056$, $\hat{\beta}_1 = -0.0645$ (both *p* < 0.001).
For Total Live Births: $\hat{\beta}_0 = 52{,}542$, $\hat{\beta}_1 = -249.5$
(both *p* < 0.001). Despite highly significant coefficients, the residuals of
this model carry strong autocorrelation for both series (see @sec-diagnostics),
invalidating the white-noise assumption.

### ARIMA Models

The general ARIMA(*p*, *d*, *q*) model for a time series $y_t$ after *d*
orders of differencing is:

$$
\phi(B)(1-B)^d y_t = \theta(B)\,\varepsilon_t
$$

where $\phi(B) = 1 - \phi_1 B - \cdots - \phi_p B^p$ is the AR polynomial,
$\theta(B) = 1 - \theta_1 B - \cdots - \theta_q B^q$ is the MA polynomial,
$B$ is the backshift operator, and
$\varepsilon_t \sim \text{WN}(0, \sigma^2)$.

**TFR — ARIMA(0,1,1):** $p = 0$, $d = 1$, $q = 1$:
$$
(1 - B)\,y_t = (1 + \theta_1 B)\,\varepsilon_t
$$
$$
y_t - y_{t-1} = \varepsilon_t - 0.799\,\varepsilon_{t-1}
$$
Estimated innovation variance: $\hat{\sigma}^2 = 0.0196$. AICc = −54.80.
This model is equivalent to simple exponential smoothing (SES) on the
differenced series with smoothing parameter $\alpha = 1 - |\theta_1| = 0.201$.

**Total Live Births — ARIMA(0,1,0):**
$$
(1 - B)\,y_t = \varepsilon_t \implies y_t - y_{t-1} = \varepsilon_t
$$
Estimated innovation variance: $\hat{\sigma}^2 = 7{,}542{,}931$. AICc = 1029.14.
This is a pure random walk; the Drift model (above) is preferred for live births
because it captures the persistent declining trend.

### ETS Model

The ETS model selected by the fable package is of the form
ETS(A, Ad, N) for TFR — additive error, damped additive trend, no seasonality:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \ell_{t-1} + \phi\,b_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t \\
\ell_t &= \ell_{t-1} + \phi\,b_{t-1} + \alpha\,\varepsilon_t \\
b_t &= \phi\,b_{t-1} + \beta\,\varepsilon_t
\end{aligned}
$$

Estimated parameters for TFR: $\alpha = 0.993$, $\beta = 0.0001$,
$\phi = 0.901$, $\ell_0 = 6.199$, $b_0 = -0.511$.
The near-unity $\alpha$ implies very fast adaptation of the level, while the
small $\beta$ and damped $\phi < 1$ produce a slowly decaying trend component.

For Total Live Births the selected ETS is ETS(A, N, N) — simple exponential
smoothing with additive error and no trend or seasonal component:
$$
y_t = \ell_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \quad \ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + \alpha\,\varepsilon_t
$$
Estimated: $\alpha = 0.890$, $\ell_0 = 61{,}570$.

## Model Selection Tables {#sec-diagnostics}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fit-stats

fit_stats <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "candidate_model_fit_statistics.csv"),
                      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(Measure, .model, AIC, AICc, BIC)
kable(fit_stats, digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ljung-box
#| tbl-cap: "Ljung-Box residual test (lag = 10)"
ljung_box <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "residual_ljung_box_tests.csv"),
                      show_col_types = FALSE)
kable(ljung_box, digits = 4,
      col.names = c("Series", "Model", "LB statistic", "p-value"))
```

```{r}

```


## Models Not Selected

The table below records the reason each non-selected candidate was rejected.

| Series | Rejected model | Main reason | Supporting evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| TFR | Naïve | Fails Ljung-Box (p < 0.001); higher RMSE than ARIMA | @tbl-ljung-box; @tbl-holdout-accuracy |
| TFR | Drift | Fails Ljung-Box (p < 0.001); RMSE = 0.318 vs ARIMA 0.178 | @tbl-ljung-box; @tbl-holdout-accuracy |
| TFR | Linear trend | Fails Ljung-Box (LB = 177.5, p < 0.001); MAPE = 93% | @tbl-ljung-box; @fig-resid-acf |
| TFR | ETS | Passes diagnostics but higher RMSE (0.190) than ARIMA (0.178) | @tbl-holdout-accuracy |
| Live Births | Naïve | Identical to ARIMA(0,1,0); lower RMSE than Drift | — |
| Live Births | ARIMA(0,1,0) | Equivalent to Naïve; Drift captures historical trend better | @tbl-holdout-accuracy |
| Live Births | ETS | Passes diagnostics but RMSE = 6,222 vs Drift 4,097 | @tbl-holdout-accuracy |
| Live Births | Linear trend | Fails Ljung-Box (LB = 109.6, p < 0.001); invalid PIs | @tbl-ljung-box |

The linear trend model deserves specific comment for Total Live Births. Its
holdout RMSE (2,719) is the lowest of all five candidates, which might suggest
it is the best model by a simple accuracy criterion. However, a model with
residual autocorrelation this severe (LB = 109.6) cannot produce valid
prediction intervals: its stated uncertainty will be systematically too narrow
(because autocorrelated residuals carry information that has not been extracted
by the model). For a forecast whose primary value is in quantifying uncertainty
as well as direction, this disqualifies the linear trend model from selection.

## Holdout Forecast Evaluation

```{r}
#| label: tbl-holdout-accuracy
#| tbl-cap: "Holdout forecast accuracy (2016–2025, all candidates)"
holdout_accuracy <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "holdout_forecast_accuracy.csv"),
                             show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(Measure, .model, ME, RMSE, MAE, MAPE, ACF1) |>
  arrange(Measure, RMSE)
kable(holdout_accuracy, digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-holdout
#| fig-cap: "Holdout forecast comparison (2016–2025)."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure_dir, "holdout_forecast_comparison.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-best-models
#| tbl-cap: "Best model per series by holdout RMSE (accuracy criterion only)"
best_holdout <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "best_holdout_models.csv"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE)
kable(best_holdout, digits = 3)
```

Note that `best_holdout_models.csv` identifies the linear trend as best for
live births by RMSE alone. The main report selects Drift instead, because the
combined accuracy-and-diagnostics criterion is the appropriate basis for model
selection (see Section 7.3 of the main report).
